transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Ysolde 3 FP, Aldous 3 FP, Morwen 3 FP, Mire 3 FP. Face-up: Rising Floodwaters [H-03], Hive-Touched Pack [T-01].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain needles down on Hollowmoot's last dry causeway as a woman half-runs, half-wades toward you, skirts sodden black to the knee — Sela, who kept the eel-traps below Wick Lane until three nights ago. Her boy Corren followed a sound none of the rest of you can hear out past the reed banks toward Saint Orrin's Drowned Temple, and hasn't come back. Behind her, the causeway itself is dying: the water already licks the third plank-step down, and by the old marks on the pilings, Gullet Ford will be underwater by tomorrow's low tide — your last one for weeks. Out past the reeds, something moves in a loose, patient line, low to the water, in no hurry at all; hooked shapes catch what little light there is. Sela grabs whichever of you stands nearest and won't let go.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: Hush. I've got you, and you're going to tell me everything. What did Corren follow into those reeds? What sound made him leave?

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde catches Sela's trembling hands and holds her steady, meeting her eyes with the focused attention that has made a dozen desperate people trust her across night-barge tables. She doesn't pull away from the fear—she leans into it, solid and present.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: Sela, stay with me. When did Corren slip away? Which way did he go—toward the temple, or into the deep reeds?

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (I grip Sela's shoulders firmly, meeting her panicked eyes through the driving rain. My gaze flickers once toward the hooked shapes moving in the reeds, then locks back on her face—steady, present.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: Your son is taken by the hive-touched, but I know how to fight what took him—that's what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen lets Sela's grip hold, eyes fixed on the shapes moving through the reeds with their hooked spears and patient, coordinated hunger. She reaches into the years the Order spent training her, into the bitter certainty of her childhood—that knowledge of how the hive-touched move, hunt, think. She's reading their patterns now, feeling the cadence of their wrongness like a spider reading vibrations on its web, preparing herself for what comes next.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Easy, Sela. I've got you—you're on solid plank now. Tell me what you saw out there. What took the boy?

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire catches Sela with a firm grip that grounds her, drawing on her training in the watch drills. She holds the line of the causeway with her body, steady and present, while her trained eye scans the reeds and the water beyond, counting the threat and marking the shapes that catch the light. She keeps Sela close but doesn't let her panic—there's work to understand first.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: Threshwick was just one mill-house—this is your son. I was trained for this, Sela, and I won't fail where the Order taught me to stand. Let me see what we're facing.

Sela's words come in a flood, matching the rain: "The bell — Saint Orrin's bell, ringing wrong, like it's underwater and singing anyway. Corren just... walked. Toward the temple, past the ford, out where the reeds get tall." She doesn't let go of whichever hand holds hers, knuckles white.

Morwen doesn't blink at the approaching shapes. Years of Order drilling click into place behind her eyes — the pack doesn't hunt like beasts, and it doesn't hunt like men. It hunts in a *rhythm*, spears lifting and falling in near-unison, like a congregation moving through a rite it no longer remembers the meaning of. She reads the pattern whole: where the gaps fall, when they close, how the ignored pain makes them slow to change direction once committed. It settles into her like doctrine — cold, useful, certain. The others feel it too, in how she suddenly stands straighter, voice low: "I know how they move. Watch the second beat — that's when they overcommit."

She reads the whole group in a glance—the same sharp empathy that's kept desperate people alive across night-barge tables—assessing who can hold and how they fit against what's coming. Her voice drops to that focused certainty that cuts through panic.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: Listen to me, Sela—the rain speaks to those who listen. We have until dawn, when low tide brings our window. We reach him before then or lose everyone.

transcript.speaker: Aldous

The causeway trembles as water climbs higher, and I read the story the deluge tells: how long it will hold, when it will release. When my eyes open, they're steady on Sela's face. I'm still gripping her shoulder, holding the line.)

transcript.text: The second beat—that's when they break. I'm going through there now.

Morwen's rite lands home on the one still standing, a shudder running through it like a rope cut mid-pull, and it folds, thrashing, into the black water. friction.text: Engine had to refuse a GM invoke on an out-of-play tag ('hooked spears and nets' on T-01) during the event-19 opposition roll, indicating the GM's tracking of which tags are currently 'in play' on the NPC card lagged the fiction.

Engine had to refuse Mire's attempt to invoke the same aspect (A-1.1.5, 'Control the Causeway') twice on a single roll (event 31), showing friction in player-side aspect-invoke bookkeeping during a tense multi-attack sequence.

All three tie results in this scene (events 19, 29, 31) resolved via improvised GM costs with no accompanying deck draw, even though the standing interim ruling for ties (AMB-19) calls for a deck draw alongside the boost — suggesting the draw step is being skipped in practice.
Two GM compels were stacked on Mire back-to-back (events 42 and 58) within the same scene, concentrating complications on one character rather than spreading them.

Event 53's consequence is labeled 'severe' while the recorded absorb value (4) matches the rules' 'moderate' tier, creating a mismatch between the stated consequence severity and its mechanical value.
None of the scene's three cost/compel events drew a card despite the scene ledger being structured around drawn-card tags, so the intended tag-flavored costs were never actually exercised.
Aldous is compelled twice in the same scene (events 75 and 83) both centered on the same 'cannot lie to a priest' bind, which may read as repetitive pressure rather than escalating stakes.

The scene stacks five accepted compels plus a hostile-trouble invoke in a single social scene, all against the same NPC (Brother Ansel) and largely the same standoff, which is a lot of fate-point-generating events for one unresolved central question.

No GM fate-point ledger is visible across the log, making it hard for the table (or an auditor) to confirm the GM never overspent; this is purely a bookkeeping/visibility issue rather than a proven rule breach.

The free invoke created by Aldous's create_advantage (event 112) is only identified in freeform notes ('aspect A-1.4.15 (1 free)') rather than in the tags_invoked field, making it hard to audit which future invokes are free vs. paid.
The GM's opposition-side aspect invoke (C-02) at event 105 has no corresponding fate-point ledger entry, leaving the GM's fate point economy for the scene untraceable from the log.

Several roleplay 'declare' events (98, 99, 101, 107, 109, 110) carry no skill or resolution data, interleaving freeform narration with mechanical rolls in a way that makes it harder to trace which fictional beats actually drove which dice results.

The tie-cost for Aldous (event 128) narratively sets him up as 'wide open,' and the very next defend roll (126) has him taking a hit from the enforcer pair — the causal link is implied by fiction but not explicitly tagged/cross-referenced in the log, making the chain a bit opaque on replay.

Both Morwen's and Mire's troubles get spent twice in quick succession (compel then hostile invoke) within the same short scene, which reads as efficient FP economy for the GM but stacks complications on the same two characters back-to-back.

Collapsing the two flanking enforcers into a single static +1 'pair' opposition for the defend roll (126) sacrifices tactical distinction between the two attackers, and it's not clear from the log whether that was a deliberate simplification or a shortcut.

free_text.best_moment: When Sister Prioress Vessa's iron certainty cracked at seeing the hive-marks fade—Ysolde reading the mercy beneath doctrine, Aldous confirming it with his supernatural sight, Morwen paying blood to crack her composure. It was everything Ysolde is: reading what people are afraid to believe, speaking to the person beneath the armor.
free_text.most_frustrating: The Cartel confrontation at the end felt rushed and action-heavy compared to the earlier reading/negotiation moments. Wish I had more space to deeply read the enforcer leader instead of falling into combat-adjacent threat posturing. Also wanted to push harder on whether Ysolde genuinely owes the Cartel or is playing that debt—felt like I dodged it rather than engaged with it.
free_text.background_used: Well-integrated. The exile, the secrets-hearing, and both Order and Cartel connections all came into play naturally. The reading-people aspect threaded through every major scene. Didn't feel forced. The specific oath against the traitor didn't come up, but what did use felt earned, not shoehorned in.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: A deeper exploration of Ysolde's actual standing with the Cartel—is she genuinely indebted or playing them? More nuanced negotiation/reading with the enforcer leader rather than the combat-framing that took over. And more opportunity to use her "hears secrets" aspect beyond reading faces—discovering something that changed how she approached later scenes.
free_text.one_sentence: My backstory as the exiled cook who reads secrets was core to how I solved every problem this session, though the specific oath against the traitor I swore remained unexplored.

free_text.best_moment: When Aldous read plain that Corren's hive-marks were fading, not spreading, and that reading broke through Sister Prioress Vessa's certainty. The character's core concept—reading truth in uncertain situations—did exactly what it exists to do and literally saved a boy's life.
free_text.most_frustrating: The compel about not lying to a priest came at the moment when Aldous needed to project absolute certainty about Corren's state. Having to voice uncertainty right before proving himself right created the right emotional beat but tugged slightly against the narrative momentum.
free_text.background_used: Excellent. Every core aspect was woven in naturally: the rain-reading as the mechanism of salvation, the drowned ghosts' marks as supernatural perception that mattered, the vow to cross souls as the mission driver, and the conflict with the Order as the central scene. It felt organic, not forced or referenced externally.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I would have liked to explore the drowned ghosts' actual voice and perspective more deeply, rather than just the mechanical perception they grant. They're mentioned often but remain somewhat abstract—I wanted to hear what they actually whisper.
free_text.one_sentence: My backstory wasn't just present but mechanically central to the story—the rain-reading was how we won, the soul-saving vow was the entire mission, and the ghost-marks manifested as perception that mattered in real moments.

free_text.best_moment: Walking past Ansel's stalled censers into the belltower, using Order training as armor against an authority I was supposed to submit to—it proved the childhood they made me wasn't wasted, even torn and weaponless and desperate.
free_text.most_frustrating: The severe consequence from the Pikemaw left me unable to stand independently for hours of play—every victory afterward felt earned but pyrrhic, watching the climax from Mire's shoulder rather than standing in it myself.
free_text.background_used: Good. Both aspects of my Order upbringing and my vow to stand against the Wardens' torches were woven throughout and earned, not forced. The Prioress activating 'Too Famous to Hide' felt organic to the world, not a gotcha—she knew my name because my name means something in the Sallowmere.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: End the session standing on my own two feet. Morwen bought her victories with blood—she broke the Prioress's certainty, saved Corren, stood against the Cartel—but she spent everything to do it, and by the final scene she was running on fumes someone else was lending her.
free_text.one_sentence: The backstory was used well—woven in organically, central to every major choice, feeling like an expression of who Morwen is rather than a trap set to punish her.

free_text.best_moment: Stepping between Morwen and the Order's censers, using militia bearing and authority-language to hold the line through presence and discipline rather than steel. That felt like Mire's exact purpose—holding ground the way she was trained, in a moment where force wouldn't have worked.
free_text.most_frustrating: Mire was strong support but not the emotional center. Her aspects—especially being a marked enemy of the Causeway Wardens—didn't get full engagement. She held the line for someone else's rescue rather than fighting for something that cuts into her own history.
free_text.background_used: Good. My Order training fired at the right moments (recognizing the hive-mark on Corren, speaking the watch-drill language to hold Brother Ansel steady, understanding militia bearing). The mortgaged house and Cartel debt activated at the end. But the specific aspect about being cast out by Captain Verrick and marked enemy of the Wardens stayed backgrounded rather than becoming a real conflict.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: A direct personal reckoning with someone who wronged Mire—especially Captain Verrick or the Causeway Wardens proper. I wanted her vengeance-nature to drive events rather than just supporting others' emotional cores, or at least have that tension come alive as a real complication.
free_text.one_sentence: My training and debt-obligations shaped key moments well and mattered when they came up, but my core conflict with the Wardens and my vengeful nature remained backgrounded rather than central to the story.

chronicle.summary: A mother's plea led the party into Saint Orrin's Drowned Temple, where Morwen's voice broke the swarm-song's hold and pulled Corren back from the hive — scarred but himself. Ysolde, Aldous, Morwen and Mire then bent Sister Prioress Vessa's iron doctrine without breaking it, buying the boy a reprieve the Order will be watching closely. Fleeing the rising flood, they talked and bled their way past Cartel enforcers at the water's edge, Aldous finding a hidden ford that carried them all out ahead of the drowning stair.
